subject: Including covariates in sem() and extracting R-square for mediation analysis

messages.author: 91f29fd6fb3b86ad
messages.subject: Including covariates in sem() and extracting R-square for mediation analysis
parts:
Hi,
I am running mediation analysis using sem().
I have a couple of questions related to including covariates in the model and extracting R-square.

1) I used the example for mediation from the tutorial (X: predictor, Y: dependent variable, M: mediator) and added new variable named Cov
I wanted to adjust for Cov in direct and mediation models. But it didn't allow me.

set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
Cov <- 0.5*X + 0.7*M +0.9*Y + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M, Cov=Cov)

model <- ' # direct effect
Y ~ c*X+d*Cov
# mediator
M ~ a*X+e*Cov
Y ~ b*M +g*Cov
# indirect effect (a*b)
ab := a*b
# total effect
total := c + (a*b)'

fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
Error in lavParseModelString(model) : 
  lavaan ERROR: duplicate model element in: Y~b*M+g*Cov

Why it didn't work?
If I took Cov from either M ~ a*X+e*Cov or Y ~ b*M +g*Cov. It worked. Do you know why?

model2 <- ' # direct effect
Y ~ c*X+d*Cov
# mediator
M ~ a*X+e*Cov
Y ~ b*M
# indirect effect (a*b)
ab := a*b
# total effect
total := c + (a*b)'

fit2 <- sem(model2, data = Data)

2) I want to extract R-square for each model (direct effect model and mediator models). How could I do it?
I used
R2.boot <- bootstrapLavaan(fit2, R=1000, FUN = lavInspect, what = "rsquare")
apply(R2.boot, 2,quantile, probs = c(.025, .975))
apply(R2.boot, 2,median)

and lavInspect(fit2,what="rsquare")
It gave values of Y and M. What are the meanings of those Y and M?

Thanks so much for your help.

I really appreciate.

Ann

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Including covariates in sem() and extracting R-square for mediation analysis
parts:
Ann,
An SE model can only have one equation for each variable.  When you include multiple equation in your model syntax, lavaan needs to combine these into one equation.  If you tell lavaan that Y ~ c*X+d*Cov and Y ~ b*M then lavaan can just combine these into one equation Y ~ c*X+d*Cov + b*M.  However, if you tell lavaan that Y ~ c*X+d*Cov
and Y ~ b*M +g*Cov then putting these together yields Y ~ c*X+d*Cov + b*M +g*Cov.  It is not possible to estimate two separate weights for Cov.  Those are the duplicate elements that lavaan is complaining about.

Y and M are both endogenous variables in your model.  So, each has its own equation and its own R-square.

Keith

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Including covariates in sem() and extracting R-square for mediation analysis
parts:
Ann,
  I need to answer your question in stages.

(1) Currently, your models are misspecified.  You simulate Cov as an endogenous outcome of the X, M, and Y but you model Cov as an exogenous cause of X, M, and Y.  As a result, your model parameter estimates are biased and you cannot really recover anything accurately.  So, I modified the simulation to match the model.

set.seed(1234)
Cov <- rnorm(100) # changed to exogenous variable
X <- .2 * Cov + rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5 * X + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M, Cov=Cov)

(2) I am not clear what you mean by two models for Y.  If you mean that you have two lines beginning "Y ~ " in your model syntax, that is true.  However, you still only have one model (equation) for Y.  Lavaan needs to combine your two lines into one equation for Y.  That is why you cannot duplicate elements across the two lines.

To see this better, look at the matrix form of the model.

> lavInspect(fit, what='free')$beta
    Y M X Cov
Y   0 3 1   2
M   0 0 4   5
X   0 0 0   0
Cov 0 0 0   0

Each element in the matrix represents the effect of the column variable on the row variable.  There is only one parameter for the effect of Cov on Y (labelled 2).  So, you can only specify one parameter to take the place of parameter 2.  Likewise, there is only one row in the table for Y.  That row represents the one and only equation for Y in the model. 

(3) Yes, I believe that it would be possible to compute those things as defined parameters.  However, the variances of endogenous variables are not parameters in the model.  So, you would first need to compute those as defined parameters.  You could then use those to compute the variance passed on through a given effect.  Finally, you could take the ratios of these to obtain something analogous to an R-square.

However, I am not sure how useful that would be.  If I am thinking about this correctly, the variances of X and Y will just cancel out of the numerator and denominator.  So, you could just look at the ratios formed from squaring the effects.

model <- ' # Duplicate label omitted

# X and Y
X ~ Cov
Y ~ c*X + d*Cov + b*M

# mediator
M ~ a*X + e*Cov

cSquare := c^2

# proportions
abProp := abSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)
cProp := cSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)

' # End model syntax
fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

summary(fit)

Here is the result for the two proportions.

    abProp            0.906    0.164    5.507    0.000
    cProp             0.094    0.164    0.574    0.566

I have never seen that done before.  So, perhaps others can chime in if I am missing something.

Keith

Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
